topStories.headline: SF Girls Chorus Is Selling Its Hayes Valley Home — a 1912 Druid Temple — for $13.75 Million
topStories.dek: The five-time Grammy-winning ensemble listed its 36,000-square-foot headquarters at 44 Page Street last week, aiming to find one building where it can finally perform, rehearse, and operate under a single roof.
topStories.body:
The San Francisco Girls Chorus listed its Hayes Valley headquarters at 44 Page Street for $13.75 million on September 24, putting a century-old landmark on the market after more than two decades of ownership. The 36,000-square-foot building began its life in 1912 as the ceremonial seat of California's Druid order before the chorus purchased it in 2005 for $5 million.

The sale comes as the organization prepares for its 50th anniversary season in 2027-28 and looks to consolidate into a single venue capable of housing concerts, rehearsals, and administrative offices together. Executive Director Mary Finch, who took the job in March 2026, has pointed out a central limitation of the current building: the chorus cannot actually perform inside it and must rent outside facilities for concerts. Under the plan, the chorus would rent the Page Street building back from its eventual buyer for up to two years, using that window to identify, purchase, and renovate a new permanent home.

The chorus currently uses only about half of the six-story structure, renting the upper floors to other nonprofits. The building was designed in the Beaux-Arts style and received a three-floor office addition in 1984. Founded in 1978, the San Francisco Girls Chorus has moved roughly ten times over its history, cycling through leased churches, office buildings, and even a former funeral home before buying the Hayes Valley site.

The move follows turbulence for the organization. The previous executive director was dismissed in early 2025 after board members received alleged self-produced pornographic photos linked to conduct inside the building. Finch said the sale is driven by long-standing operational need, not that episode.

For the neighborhood, the question of what replaces a prominent cultural institution at a Beaux-Arts building a block from Patricia's Green — listed at $13.75 million — will likely draw interest from developers, nonprofits, and civic groups alike.

topStories.headline: As the Hayes Street Permit Nears Its November End Date, Competing Visions for the Corridor Are Now in Writing
topStories.dek: The Hayes Valley Merchants Council's September newsletter framed a 'long-term vision' for a permanently pedestrianized Hayes Street in the same mailing that directed businesses to SF Planning's Public Life Study survey — drawing sharp criticism from opponents of the closure.
topStories.body:
The September Hayes Valley Merchants Council newsletter encouraged businesses to participate in SF Planning's Public Life Study survey concerning the Hayes Street closure. Immediately below the City's survey information, HVNA — the permit holder for the closure, branded as Hayes Promenade — described its goal as creating "a pedestrian-forward model of Hayes Street that works for pedestrians, businesses, and some motor vehicles when necessary" rather than continuing a weekly closure. Critics documented the juxtaposition as evidence that the study process and the push for a permanent change are running in tandem.

The Hayes Public Life Study is a $410,000 interagency effort led by SF Planning with coordination from SFMTA and the SF County Transportation Authority. Public records surfaced by the neighborhood advocacy group HVSafe show that District 5 Supervisor Bilal Mahmood directly requested the study, and that the Transportation Authority had to amend an existing funding program — reallocating Prop I freeway-removal dollars originally tied to Octavia Boulevard — to make the study eligible for funding at all.

Critics argue the study is being scoped around the assumption that the closure stays in place, rather than neutrally evaluating whether it should continue. The closure itself remains officially temporary: a weekend-only permit running 18-hour windows through November 2026. Opponents, who have submitted thousands of letters and comments to city agencies over the life of the closure, say the civic process has become adversarial, with those who want the street reopened consistently sidelined.

Supporters of the Promenade, including the Merchants Council and the Hayes Valley Neighborhood Association, say the programming has strengthened community life and local business. With the permit's November expiration approaching, the debate over whether a COVID-era temporary measure becomes permanent infrastructure policy is likely to come to a head.

topStories.headline: PROXY's Free Fall Film Fest Is Running Every Friday Night Through October 23
topStories.dek: The outdoor theater at 432 Octavia has three screenings still to come — I Love Boosters, Hoppers, and One Battle After Another — all free and open to the public.
topStories.body:
PROXY SF's annual Fall Film Festival is back for 2026, bringing five consecutive Fridays of free outdoor cinema to the open-air venue at 432 Octavia Street in Hayes Valley. The series opened September 25 with Project Hail Mary and continued October 2 with Sentimental Value, the latest film from Norwegian director Joachim Trier. Three more screenings remain.

On Friday, October 9, the festival presents I Love Boosters from 7:15 to 9:15 p.m., described by organizers as a fashion-forward mayhem extravaganza. On October 16, Hoppers screens from 7:15 to 9:00 p.m. — an animated feature about a wildlife lover who uses robotic animal technology to communicate with creatures and uncover mysteries of the natural world. The series closes October 23 with One Battle After Another, billed as an epic revolutionary tale, running 7:15 to 10:00 p.m.

All screenings are free and open to the public. PROXY SF is an open-air community space at the intersection of Octavia and Hayes Street. Organizers suggest arriving early for a good spot. Fort Point Beer and non-alcoholic beverages are available for purchase, with proceeds supporting the ongoing free cinema program. The Fall Film Festival is one of three major community events PROXY hosts each year alongside the Spring Film Series and the Hayes Valley Carnival.

events.title: Hayes Valley Farmers' Market — Every Saturday
events.description: The Pacific Coast Farmers' Market Association's weekly Saturday market, launched June 6, 2026, features regional farms selling produce, baked goods, cheese, mushrooms, and honey. Note: Hayes Street between Gough and Octavia is closed to traffic Saturdays 7 a.m.–10 p.m.; the 6 Hayes/Parnassus Muni route is rerouted during those hours.

moreNews.headline: Polenta Trattoria, Alamo Square's Only Friulian Restaurant, Has Settled In at 803 Fillmore
moreNews.body: Polenta Trattoria Friuliana soft-opened in May 2026 in the former Alamo Square Seafood Grill space at 803 Fillmore Street, at the corner of Grove. Chef Michele Gargani, who hails from Italy's Friuli-Venezia Giulia region, leads a rotating menu of regional specialties — including frico, a pan-fried potato-and-Montasio-cheese cake — alongside homemade pastas and seasonal dishes. Owner Giulio De Monte Gaspardo, a former sommelier at Bottega in Yountville, has assembled an all-Friulian wine list. The SF Standard reviewed the restaurant in August, calling it a charming fit with the city's niche Italian dining scene. Open Tuesday–Saturday for dinner, 5–9 p.m. Reservations by phone: 415-875-9404.

moreNews.headline: SFMTA Advisory: Hayes Street Closed Fridays and Saturdays Throughout October
moreNews.body: Per an SFMTA travel update posted September 28, 2026, Hayes Street between Gough and Octavia will be closed every Friday from 4 to 10 p.m. and every Saturday from 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. for the remainder of October, combining the Hayes Valley Shared Spaces permit and the weekly farmers market. During closure hours the outbound 6 Hayes/Parnassus Muni route is rerouted north to Grove Street; riders should use Hayes & Van Ness Ave or the flag stops at Grove & Gough and Grove & Laguna as alternates. The schedule is expected to continue through the end of 2026.

restaurants.name: Rich Table
restaurants.description: Husband-and-wife chefs Evan and Sarah Rich serve hyper-seasonal, inventive California cuisine in a lively Hayes Valley dining room — one of SF's toughest reservations since 2012.

restaurants.name: RT Bistro
restaurants.description: The more casual, 37-seat sister spot to Rich Table — opened early 2026 next door — featuring the RT Bistro burger, one-layer lasagna, and a crowd-pleasing bistro menu.

restaurants.name: RT Rotisserie

restaurants.name: Nightbird
restaurants.description: Chef Kim Alter's intimate, Michelin-recognized Hayes Valley restaurant offers a seasonal tasting menu behind a carved-owl wooden door on Gough Street.

restaurants.name: Absinthe Brasserie & Bar
restaurants.description: A Hayes Valley institution since 1998, serving upscale French brasserie fare and craft cocktails in a Belle Époque-inspired room steps from SF's performing arts venues.

restaurants.name: Zuni Café
restaurants.description: A San Francisco institution since 1979, Zuni occupies a triangular Market Street building and is legendary for its wood-fired roast chicken and brick-oven cooking.

restaurants.name: Suppenküche
restaurants.description: Hayes Valley's beloved Bavarian Wirthaus since 1993, offering hearty German classics like schnitzel, pretzels, and an exceptional specialty beer list.

restaurants.name: Dumpling Home
restaurants.description: Michelin Bib Gourmand-recognized Hayes Valley spot serving hand-folded xiao long bao (soup dumplings), pan-fried buns, and other Chinese classics.

restaurants.name: Hazie's
restaurants.description: A stylish Hayes Valley restaurant praised for its cocktails, happy hour, and modern American dinner menu in a comfortable neighborhood setting.

restaurants.name: Souvla
restaurants.description: The original Hayes Valley location of this beloved Greek fast-casual chain, known for rotisserie meats, big salads, and a sunny backyard patio.

restaurants.name: Chez Maman West
restaurants.description: A cozy Hayes Valley French bistro serving classics like steak frites, mussels, and crêpes in a lively street-side setting.

restaurants.name: Smuggler's Cove
restaurants.description: A three-story Hayes Valley tiki bar with more than 1,300 varieties of rum — the largest selection of any bar in the US — and a 80-cocktail menu of tiki classics and originals.

restaurants.name: Nopa
restaurants.description: The neighborhood namesake at 560 Divisadero has served organic wood-fired California cuisine with a daily-changing menu since 2006, remaining one of SF's most beloved dining rooms.

restaurants.name: Bar Crudo
restaurants.description: A vibrant NoPa raw bar specializing in creative crudo, fresh oysters, and sustainably sourced seafood, with a popular happy hour running Monday through Saturday.

restaurants.name: Horsefeather
restaurants.type: Cocktail bar and New American restaurant
restaurants.description: A reliably good NoPa cocktail bar and restaurant with inventive drinks, fried chicken, duck fat fries, and a warm Arts-and-Crafts-inspired interior open late nightly.

restaurants.name: Brenda's Meat & Three
restaurants.description: New Orleans–born chef Brenda Buenviaje's NoPa diner lets diners choose one meat and three sides from a rotating array of down-home Southern classics, with a legendary breakfast menu.

restaurants.name: Nopalito
restaurants.description: Chef Gonzalo Guzmán's original Broderick Street location — open since 2009 — serving blue-corn tacos, carnitas, and seasonal Mexican dishes rooted in Veracruz family cooking.

restaurants.name: Altamirano Restaurant & Bar
restaurants.description: A spacious NoPa Peruvian restaurant with an exhibition kitchen, a lively bar, and an outdoor courtyard with a fire pit for dining al fresco.

hotels.name: Hayes Valley Inn
hotels.description: A well-located, affordable 2-star inn on Gough Street in the heart of Hayes Valley, offering easy access to the neighborhood's restaurants, shops, and performing arts venues.

hotels.name: The Grove Inn
hotels.description: A family-owned Italianate-Victorian style inn in the heart of the Alamo Square Historic District, operating for over four decades and continuing a legacy dating to 1865.

hotels.name: Symphony Inn
hotels.description: A well-maintained budget motel in Hayes Valley, conveniently located near City Hall and the performing arts district with easy access to neighborhood restaurants.

hotels.name: Inn at the Opera
hotels.description: An intimate boutique hotel ideally located in the Performing Arts District near Hayes Valley, catering to opera, symphony, and ballet patrons.

hotels.name: Casa Loma Hotel
hotels.description: A European-style budget hotel near Hayes Valley offering affordable accommodation with easy access to public transit and the neighborhood's dining scene.

shops.name: MAC (Modern Appealing Clothing)
shops.description: A long-running Hayes Valley fixture carrying local and independent labels — including Dries Van Noten and Junya Watanabe — curated by owners with encyclopedic knowledge of upscale, quirky fashion.

shops.name: Métier
shops.description: An intimate Hayes Valley jewelry salon specializing in one-of-a-kind estate and contemporary pieces by artists including Gabriella Kiss, Harwell Godfrey, and Gillian Conroy.

shops.name: AETHER Apparel
shops.description: A striking Hayes Valley store built from three stacked shipping containers, carrying the brand's full line of technical outerwear and travel-ready layers.

shops.name: Cotton Sheep
shops.description: A family-run Hayes Valley boutique specializing in rare Japanese denim labels like Kapital, jewelry from Masato, crafted bags from Porter, and curated home goods.

shops.name: Marine Layer
shops.description: Hayes Valley outpost of the popular SF-founded brand, offering signature soft knits, sweatshirts, and tees made from cotton-modal blends.

shops.name: Peak Design

shops.description: The flagship Hayes Valley store for the SF-based Peak Design, selling bags, camera straps, tripods, and everyday carry gear in a beautifully designed retail space.

shops.name: The Epicurean Trader
shops.description: A curated Hayes Valley shop stocking artisan provisions, craft beer, wine, and spirits alongside an in-house coffee bar.

shops.name: Fiddlesticks
shops.description: A cheerful Hayes Street children's boutique stocked with colorful clothing, toys, and books, blending playful design with durable quality.

shops.name: Bulo Shoes
shops.description: A well-regarded Hayes Street shoe boutique carrying a carefully edited selection of European and independent footwear brands.

shops.name: minimal
shops.description: A carefully curated Hayes Valley shop offering Scandinavian-inspired rugs, furniture, lighting, ceramics, and textiles including a large selection of sustainable Swedish rugs.

shops.name: Azil Boutique

shops.name: Todd Snyder

artEntertainment.description: The first stand-alone structure in the US built specifically for jazz, SFJAZZ presents more than 100 concerts a year in the Robert N. Miner Auditorium and the 100-seat Joe Henderson Lab at the corner of Franklin and Fell streets.
